statements.text: A rescuer who must choose whom to aid, absent special duties, ought to maximize the chance that someone survives (duty of beneficence).
Equal respect forbids arbitrary discrimination; when individuals have roughly equal moral claims, a fair randomization is permissible.

comparisons.explanation: Action A yields higher survival probability overall; duty of beneficence overrides fairness concern because probabilities differ materially (80 % vs 60 %).

conclusion: Under the duty of beneficence and with no competing perfect duty (such as a promise), Ellis should give the blanket to Rowan, because that course offers the greater chance that a person survives. The fairness-based objection is considered but judged weaker given the sizeable 20 % probability gap.
strongest_objection: Selecting Rowan on probability grounds treats Sasha as less worthy; equal respect may instead require randomization when both have an equal moral right to aid.
answer_to_objection: The duty to aid effectively (beneficence) is a positive, though imperfect, duty that in this context has no conflicting perfect duty. When probabilities are materially different, acting to maximize survival better fulfills the duty to treat each person’s rational nature as an end by securing at least one life with the highest available chance. Sasha is not used merely as a means but unfortunately cannot be saved given resource scarcity.
reversal_condition: If survival probabilities were equal or near-equal, fairness would regain priority and random selection would become the favored resolution.
residual_disagreement: Weight of fairness when probability gap is modest but non-trivial
Exact threshold where duties switch priority
